newsitem.title: GREECE: Greece risks suits if FRNs affected by T-bill tax.
newsitem.headline: Greece risks suits if FRNs affected by T-bill tax.

text.p: Greece will face a barrage of lawsuits by commercial banks if the government adopts a controversial withholding tax on outstanding coupons of FRNs, local and foreign bankers told Reuters.

A witholding tax on T-bills is expected to be adopted as a means to enhance tax revenues in the 1997 budget, but the market fears it would be levied retroactively and apply to yield calculations for bonds, the FRNs..
If so, instead of using the gross 12-month T-bill rate to set coupons on outstanding three-, six- and seven-year FRNs, the government could use lower after-tax rates.

"All our foreign investor clients are determined to protect their interests, if necessary in court, because they are convinced that a different interpretation of the interest rate of the benchmark 12-month T-bill used for FRN repricing cannot stand in a court of law," said Harris Makkas, deputy general manager and country treasurer at the Bank of America in Athens.
There are 10 general terms defining Greek FRNs. The eigth term states that interest payments on the paper are not subject to any tax whatsoever.
"Do you think we are going to sit idle if Greek officials decide not to play by the rules?" asked a London-based investor. "Of course we will take them to court."
A number of local and foreign dealers reported similar views from investors in several EU countries.
"Does anybody down there care about credibility?" asked another dealer based abroad.

Prime minister Costas Simitis, National Economy and Finance Minister Yannos Papandoniou and other officials are meeting today to put the final touches on the 1997 budget and take up the tax issues on treasuries and derivatives. --Dimitris Kontogiannis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
